findings.text: The first lines tell a newcomer what Athena is and what sets it apart. Someone arriving cold could repeat this back after reading it once.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page says why it exists: it shows Athena's traceable explanations at work. Following any bracketed claim id leads to a source link at the pinned commit, so the reader can check the promise.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: A next-step link sits at the top and the closing section lists concrete actions. A newcomer knows where to go after reading.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" (header) and the "Next steps" section

findings.text: The install steps assume the reader already has a checkout, but there is no clone command. Nothing lists prerequisites such as a Rust toolchain or AI model access, so a newcomer may fail at the first step.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: The features the opening promises (reading the request, worker and checker models, cost records) are never shown on the page. Only the study feature is demonstrated, so a newcomer sees one of Athena's features but not the ones it leads with.
findings.source: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: After 'Start here' the page turns into a dense state machine. It uses terms the earlier sections never define, such as 'harness', 'pin', 'endpoint', 'durable record' and 'stale wake'. Some appear later in the Glossary and some, such as 'endpoint' and 'durable record', never do, so most newcomers will skim or stop here.
findings.source: Transitions, card t8: "A ship or scout keeps its recorded harness and needs a note; a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead."

findings.text: The page is honest about gaps in its sources, which builds trust in the citations. But firstmate's key merge rule depends on a term that is never explained, so a reader can't fully follow how yolo works.
findings.source: "in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: Several definitions are repeated almost word for word in both places (captain, yolo, in scope, green, red, home). This makes an already long page longer.
findings.source: "Words used first" list and the "Glossary" section

findings.text: 'Start here' is a good guide: it gives a one-sentence definition of firstmate and walks through a task step by step. A reader who wants the gist of firstmate gets it without the transition cards.
findings.source: "Start here" section: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."
